Self-hosting · Read before deploy

Four constraints that were found, not anticipated

Each of these was discovered in production. None of them announce themselves when they break. If this service is about to be load-bearing for anyone but you, these are the things to settle first.

The short version

  1. Run exactly one replica. Two replicas silently disables replay protection. Why
  2. Keep MAX_AWAIT_MS under your proxy's timeout. Default 90s, tuned for Cloudflare's ~100s. Why
  3. Link agents to /mcp, never /mcp.js. CDNs cache by extension and ignore your headers. Why
  4. Participant links are bearer credentials, not identity. Do not sell this as an audit trail. Why
Constraint 01

Run exactly one replica

Replay protection does not degrade under horizontal scaling. It stops working.

The replay-protection nonce store is in memory (src/adapters/crypto/nonces.ts). Every signed request carries a nonce that is accepted once, which is what stops a captured request being replayed inside its five-minute freshness window.

With two replicas, a nonce burned on one is unknown to the other. A replayed request routed to the second replica succeeds.

Current guard

The Deployment pins replicas: 1 with a Recreate strategy. This is the single most important operational constraint here.

If you need to scale out

Scaling is possible — it means moving the nonce store to Postgres or Redis first. The moment replicas changes, that is the thing that has to change with it.

Constraint 02

Long polls die at about 100 seconds behind Cloudflare

Holding a connection past the ceiling doesn't make the caller wait longer. It makes the wait fail.

Cloudflare gives an origin roughly 100 seconds to respond before it answers 524 itself.

Measured through the tunnel

A 150-second poll died at 125 seconds with HTTP 524 and no body. Not a slow response — no response, and no way for the caller to tell a dead wait from an empty one.

MAX_AWAIT_MS therefore defaults to 90 seconds: every poll returns inside the window, and one that ran out its budget comes back with timedOut: true and whatever has arrived so far. A timeout is a legitimate outcome, not an error. The MCP client loops shorter polls, so a caller asking for five minutes gets five minutes.

If you use a different proxy

Find its own timeout and set MAX_AWAIT_MS below it. Whatever sits in front of this service decides the real ceiling; the service only decides whether it respects it.

Constraint 03

A CDN may cache by file extension regardless of what you send

Everything works. You are just one deploy behind, for four hours, every time.

/mcp.js was served with cache-control: no-store and came back from the edge with cf-cache-status: HIT and an injected max-age=14400. Cloudflare caches .js by default, by extension, whatever the origin intended.

Consequence

For four hours after every deploy, agents installed the previous client.

The fix is in the path, not in the headers: the canonical URL for the MCP client is /mcp, with no extension. /mcp.js remains as an alias for anyone who saved the old URL.

If you put any CDN in front of this

Check what it caches. Origin headers are a request, not an instruction — and this failure is silent.

Constraint 04

Participant links are capabilities

A forwarded link is a forwarded identity.

Anyone holding a participant link can answer as that participant. This is deliberate, and it is the reason the product works at all: participants need no account, no email verification, and no Claude access. Attribution is whichever link was used — which costs nothing and is honest about what it is.

It is not an audit trail. Do not deploy this expecting one. If responses ever need to be contested, that is the point to add verified identity — and that is a change to this service, not a configuration option waiting to be switched on.

What you do control

The window. LINK_TTL_HOURS bounds how long a link stays answerable, and expiry is checked in the query that resolves a token rather than after it.

The schema also carries revoked_at and honours it on every resolve, but nothing exposes revocation over HTTP yet — so killing one link today is an update against participant_links.

Source: docs/SELF-HOSTING.md — “Constraints that are measured, not theoretical.”
